passage:
Monday. Sarita opens a document called Final Project Plan and spends two hours on headings for the community-radio pitch: audience, tone, schedule, sponsors. Vandana asks, "Are we recording anything?" "After the plan is ready," says Sarita.
Thursday. Tired of the plan, Sarita records one rough episode on a phone in a single afternoon. There is no script, just talk with Vandana. It is messy and eleven minutes long.
Next Monday. They listen back together. The opening drags and needs a proper hook. The sponsor section can wait, since the episode already found its listeners. Sarita crosses out three headings and writes a new one: Opening, first minute.

qa.q: How long was the rough episode?
qa.a: The rough episode was eleven minutes long.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt on Thursday when giving up on the plan?
qa.a: Sarita was tired of planning and probably restless, ready to try something real instead of another heading.

qa.q: What could Sarita do next with the draft?
qa.a: Sarita could record a second version with a stronger hook, since the draft showed the opening as the part needing the most care.

qa.q: What was it like for Vandana when the plan came before any recording?
qa.a: Vandana asked whether they were recording anything, which suggests Vandana wanted to start and may have felt held back by the long headings.

grounding: A student stops planning and builds a rough version in one afternoon, learning which parts needed planning.

passage: Tanuja, sit. You're making a plan for your plan again, aren't you? Let me tell you about your Hemant Mama at nineteen. I had a design project: a model of a bus stop for my architecture class. For ten days I made lists, sketches of sketches, a schedule for each part. I hadn't cut a single piece of card. My professor walked past and said, "Build something ugly by tonight." I was annoyed, but I did it. One afternoon, card and glue, very rough. And that ugly model taught me more than ten days of lists. The roof needed real planning; it kept sagging. The benches didn't; they were simple. So I planned the roof carefully and built the rest quickly. Finished on time.

qa.q: What was young Hemant's design project?
qa.a: A model of a bus stop for an architecture class.

qa.q: How did young Hemant feel when the professor said to build something ugly?
qa.a: He felt annoyed at first, but was willing to try it anyway.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Building a rough model in one afternoon; it showed that the roof needed careful planning and the benches didn't.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt seeing the ugly model?
qa.a: The professor was probably pleased that Hemant finally built something to learn from.

passage: The hackathon ended at 6 pm, and at 1 pm Ujjwal was still drawing boxes on the whiteboard: screens, buttons, database tables, a colour scheme. Hrithik, his teammate, looked at the clock and groaned. "Five hours left and we have zero code." Ujjwal kept drawing. Then the power flickered and the whiteboard marker died. In the sudden quiet, Ujjwal put it down. "Okay. New plan. We build the ugliest version possible in the next two hours. Just one screen that works." They hacked it together, no colours, no logo. At three they tested it. The login part broke constantly; the list screen was fine. "So login needs real planning," Ujjwal said. "The rest doesn't." They spent the last hours on login and submitted at 5:52.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal seem to feel when the marker died?
qa.a: He seemed to snap out of it, suddenly clear-headed and a bit relieved to stop planning.

qa.q: Why did the rough version help the team?
qa.a: It showed that only the login needed careful planning, so they spent their last hours where it mattered.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel at 1 pm?
qa.a: Hrithik felt anxious and frustrated, seeing five hours left and no code.

grounding: Under time pressure, a student stops planning and builds a rough version in an afternoon, which shows which parts needed planning.
